payload.title: The Glass Hour
payload.debrief:
The file was designed around a distinction: opportunity is not identity. The key log and witness account are meaningful, but each has a limitation. The voice note offers a plausible alternative without proving it.

There is no hidden “correct juror” score. Strong reasoning addresses the best evidence against its own conclusion. A majority is a shared judgment, not a new fact.
payload.parties: The fictional state v. Alex Vale · Alleged gallery theft
payload.summary:
At 9:41 pm, the lights went out at the Halden Gallery. Eleven minutes later, the lights returned. A glass sculpture called Still Water did not.

Gallery technician Alex Vale had a service key, a disputed invoice, and a reason to be in the building. A visitor says she saw Alex carrying a covered object toward the loading bay. Alex says it was a broken projector.

The prosecution calls it a planned theft. The defense calls it an assumption built around a familiar face. Six jurors must decide what the evidence actually proves.

evidence.title: The access log
evidence.caution: Access establishes opportunity. It does not independently identify who carried the key.
evidence.content:
21:32 — Service key S-04 opens the side door.
21:39 — S-04 opens the west service corridor.
21:47 — S-04 opens the loading bay.

S-04 was assigned to Alex Vale. The facilities manager confirms that staff sometimes leave shared keys in an unlocked drawer. The log records a key identifier, not the person holding it.

evidence.title: A witness in the rain
evidence.source: Statement of Mara Chen · next morning
evidence.caution: Distinguish an observation (coat and covered object) from an inference (identity and contents).
evidence.content:
“I was waiting for a taxi across the road. Someone came out in a dark green coat. I thought it was Alex — I had seen them earlier. They were carrying something under a gray cloth.

It was raining quite hard. I could not see their face. I could not tell you what was underneath the cloth.”

The witness was about 24 metres from the loading bay.
evidence.summary: A familiar coat, seen through glass.

evidence.title: Eleven missing minutes
evidence.caution: The coverage gap supports several routes. An unobserved route is not proof that it was used.
evidence.content:
The west camera and loading-bay camera share a power circuit. Both stop recording at 21:41. The main entrance stays on a separate backup circuit.

A service passage links the sculpture room to both the loading bay and the staff stairwell. The stairwell is not monitored. The plan is a reconstruction supplied for this fictional case.
evidence.summary: The blind spot connects more than one exit.

evidence.title: The last voice note
evidence.caution: The message fits the projector account, but does not verify what was actually removed.
evidence.content:
Transcript — 12 seconds

“Hi, it’s Alex. The replacement is in. I’m taking the old one out through the bay. Can you confirm when the invoice will be paid? Call me tomorrow.”

The attachment metadata places the recording before the outage. “The old one” is not named. No audio recording is available; this is an interactive transcript visualization.

payload.question: Has the case established that Alex Vale stole Still Water?
payload.subtitle: A missing sculpture. An eleven-minute silence.

payload.title: The Last Light
payload.debrief: This file separates an immediate safety decision from the quality of earlier preparation. You can accept the need to shut down and still question whether the installation met the promise. A useful discussion makes both questions explicit.
payload.parties: Lumen Events v. Northline Studio · Contract dispute
payload.summary:
Lumen Events hired Northline Studio to install a rooftop light display for a one-night festival. The contract described a “weather-ready installation.” When rain intensified, Northline shut the display down before the headline performance.

Lumen wants its fee returned. Northline says a safe shutdown was essential and the contract did not guarantee operation in severe weather.

evidence.title: A carefully worded promise
evidence.caution: Read the promise and exception together; neither sentence automatically cancels the other.
evidence.content:
“Northline will supply a weather-ready rooftop installation operating from 19:00 to 23:00. Operation remains subject to on-site electrical safety assessment.”

No rainfall threshold is defined. Lumen signed without requesting an operational weather standard.

evidence.title: The crew chief’s account
evidence.caution: A necessary shutdown can coexist with inadequate preparation.
evidence.content: “I saw water inside the connector housing. We had taped it as instructed. I called Northline’s lead, and they said shut everything down. We had no replacement cover on site.”
evidence.summary: Water where it should not have been.

evidence.title: The rooftop layout
evidence.caution: The diagram supports a preparation issue but does not establish what rain conditions were anticipated.
evidence.content: The main control housing was under a canopy. The final connector was at the edge of the roof beyond the canopy. The supplier’s installation guide recommends a sealed enclosure for exposed outdoor connections.

evidence.title: Before the storm
evidence.caution: The phrase “normal showers” is subjective. Avoid treating an undefined term as a measurable guarantee.
evidence.content:
Lumen: “The forecast says showers. Are we okay?”
Northline: “Normal showers, yes. Anything unsafe and we stop. We’ll bring the outdoor kit.”

This fictional transcript has no attached recording.

payload.question: Did Northline Studio fail to meet its agreement with Lumen Events?
payload.subtitle: A rooftop promise. A city left in the dark.

payload.title: The Silent Platform
payload.debrief: The key tension is between an observable action and an inferred intention. A bag was taken; whether the camera was knowingly taken is a separate question. Careful jurors identify the missing link and weigh alternative explanations consistently.
payload.parties: The fictional state v. Robin Ellis · Alleged theft
payload.summary:
At a quiet station, passenger Robin Ellis picked up a navy bag and walked away. The owner of a near-identical bag later reported a missing camera. Robin returned a bag to lost property the next morning, saying it was an honest mistake.

The camera was not inside. A station attendant remembers two people near the bags, but only one appears clearly on camera.

evidence.title: The lost-property receipt
evidence.caution: Returning the bag supports a mistake account but does not establish when the camera disappeared.
evidence.content: 08:30 — Navy canvas bag received from Robin Ellis. Contents: scarf, paperback, empty camera sleeve. Robin states that the wrong bag was collected from the platform.
evidence.summary: A returned bag without a camera.

evidence.title: The attendant remembers
evidence.caution: Another person’s presence creates a possibility, not proof of another theft.
evidence.content: “There was someone else near those bags while I was helping a passenger. I did not see them touch anything. Then Robin left. The bags looked the same from where I was.”

evidence.title: A partial view
evidence.caution: A clear image of departure is not a clear image of intent.
evidence.content: Camera A covers the stairs. A structural pillar blocks the bench. Robin can be seen leaving with a bag; the footage cannot show which bag was collected or what happened at the bench.
evidence.summary: The bench is behind a pillar.

evidence.title: A call on the way home
evidence.caution: The comment could fit an unnoticed bag swap. It cannot prove Robin’s state of mind.
evidence.content:
“I’m on my way. Can you check if I left my notebook at home? I can’t find it in my bag. I’ll look properly when I get in.”

The call was logged at 22:23. No original audio is available in this fictional file.

payload.question: Does the evidence prove that Robin Ellis knowingly took the camera?
